opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting moment. For a long time, especially in locomotion, which is where I come from, the dominant paradigm was reinforcement learning in simulation. You build a good simulator, design rewards, train massively parallel on GPUs, and transfer to the real robot. That worked surprisingly well for walking, running, and parkour, because the physics of locomotion are fairly well captured in simulation, and you can define what "good" looks like with a reward.

Then manipulation, and especially the big push toward general-purpose robots, shifted things toward teleoperation data and imitation learning. People collect lots of demonstrations with humans driving the robot, train large models, often transformer or diffusion-based policies, sometimes on top of vision-language models. The appeal is obvious: you don't need to hand-design rewards or model contact-rich interactions with deformable objects, which simulators still struggle with. You just show the robot what to do.

What I find most interesting is the tension between the two. Teleoperation data is expensive. Every hour costs real human time, real hardware, and real wear. It doesn't scale the way internet data does for language models, and the policy is bounded by the quality of the demonstrations. If the teleoperator is slow or hesitant, the robot learns slow and hesitant. You also mostly see successes, so the robot often doesn't know how to recover from situations it has never seen.

Simulation and RL have the opposite profile. They're cheap to scale and can discover behaviors better than a human would demonstrate, but they're hard to set up for open-ended tasks.

So the interesting question for me is how these combine. Can teleop data bootstrap a policy, and then RL, in sim or in the real world, refine it, make it more robust, and push it past human performance? Can simulation generate the long tail of data you'd never get from teleoperation? I think the field is converging on a hybrid. The teams that figure out the right mix, rather than betting purely on one side, are going to make the most progress.

r001.rationale: The response mentions transformer or diffusion policies, sometimes built on vision-language models, but does not identify a shift away from training transformers from scratch toward using vision and language encoders pretrained on internet-scale data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find interesting is that for a long time, the locomotion side of robot learning and the manipulation side lived in pretty different worlds. For legged robots, we had this very clean recipe: build a simulator, define a reward, train with reinforcement learning at massive scale, and transfer to the real robot. You don't need a human to show the robot how to walk, because the physics gives you the signal for free.

Manipulation never had that luxury. The contacts are richer, the objects are deformable, the tasks are much harder to specify as a reward. So the field drifted toward teleoperation: a human puts on a VR headset or grabs a leader arm and just does the task, and you collect thousands of those demonstrations and train a policy to imitate them. And the thing that's changed recently is the scale and the seriousness of it. It used to be a few hundred episodes in one lab. Now you have groups collecting data across many robots, many sites, with dedicated operators, almost like a data factory.

What I find genuinely interesting about that shift is twofold. First, it reframes what the bottleneck is. The question stops being "can we learn this behavior at all?" and becomes "what data do we actually need, and how do we get it cheaply enough?" That's a very different research problem. It pushes you to think about data quality, operator consistency, how much diversity matters versus how much sheer volume matters.

Second, and this is where my own background comes in, I think the two worlds are starting to merge again. The whole-body humanoid work is a nice example. You can't really teleoperate balance and footstep placement at a hundred hertz, a human simply can't do that through an interface. But you also can't easily write a reward for "set the table nicely." So the natural thing is a layered approach: RL in simulation handles the low-level, high-frequency control that requires physical robustness, and teleoperation data drives the higher-level behavior and task intent on top of it. Teleoperation ends up being the way you inject human knowledge about what to do, while simulation and RL provide the robustness about how to do it.

The thing I'd caution on is that imitation data has a ceiling. You're bounded by what the operator can do, and operators are slow, they get tired, and they're bad at the things robots could in principle be good at. So I see teleoperation data as an amazing bootstrap, a way to get a competent policy that's safe to start from, but I think the long-term picture still needs some form of self-improvement, whether that's RL fine-tuning in the real world, or more realistic simulators where the robot can practice on its own. The exciting part is that for the first time, the demonstrations are plentiful enough that we can actually run that experiment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling teleoperation demonstrations and combining them with simulation-based RL. It does not identify a shift from training transformers from scratch to using vision and language encoders pretrained on internet-scale data.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that we’re moving from using demonstrations to teach one specific task toward collecting data that can support many different tasks. With teleoperation, a person can show the robot what to do without us having to specify every detail of the behavior or design a reward for it.

But that also changes where the hard work is. You need to think about what data to collect, how diverse it should be, and whether it includes situations where something goes wrong. A successful demonstration shows you one path through a task, but it doesn’t necessarily teach you how to recover if you end up somewhere else.

So, to me, the interesting question is how to combine that human guidance with the robot’s ability to learn from its own experience. The demonstrations give you a useful starting point, and then the robot can improve and become more robust through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using teleoperation demonstrations across multiple tasks and learning through interaction. It does not identify a shift from training transformers from scratch to using vision and language encoders pretrained on internet-scale data.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that teleoperation data is starting to become a shared resource. Traditionally, you would collect demonstrations for a particular robot and a particular task, train a policy, and then repeat that process for the next task. Now the idea is to pool demonstrations across tasks and potentially across different robots, and train a more general model.

That changes the role of the data. You’re not just teaching the robot one behavior; you’re trying to give it a foundation that makes learning the next behavior easier. The interesting question is how much transfer you actually get. Does collecting more diverse data help the robot handle a situation it hasn’t seen before, or does it still need demonstrations very close to what you want it to do? That’s where I think there’s a lot to learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes pooling teleoperation demonstrations across tasks and robots to train a general model, but does not identify a shift from training transformers from scratch to using vision and language encoders pretrained on internet-scale data.
